title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
summary: Facing a severe fiscal and balance of payments crisis in 1991, India adopted the New Economic Policy based on liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation. This chapter explains the background of the crisis, stabilisation and structural reform measures, the reforms in industry, finance, taxation, foreign exchange and trade, privatisation and disinvestment, the role of the WTO and outsourcing, and a critical appraisal of the results of the reforms.

notes.heading: Background: the economic crisis of 1991
notes.html:
• Fiscal imbalance: government expenditure, much of it on non-development items, persistently exceeded revenue. Large borrowing raised interest payments and the fiscal deficit.
  • Balance of payments crisis: imports grew much faster than exports; foreign exchange earned was not enough to pay for imports and interest on foreign debt. By 1991 foreign exchange reserves fell to a level that could finance imports for only about two weeks.
  • Rise in prices: inflation was high, partly due to deficit financing, hurting the common man.
  • External shocks: the Gulf War (1990–91) raised crude oil prices and cut remittances from the Gulf; the collapse of the Soviet Union, a major trading partner, added to difficulties; non-resident Indians withdrew deposits and confidence fell.
  • Poor performance of public enterprises which were not generating income to finance growth.

India approached the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD, World Bank) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and received a loan of about US$7 billion. In return they expected India to liberalise and open up the economy. In July 1991 the government announced the New Economic Policy (NEP).

notes.heading: Stabilisation and structural reform measures
notes.html:
Stabilisation measuresStructural reform measures
Short-termLong-term
Aimed at correcting the weaknesses in the balance of payments and bringing inflation under controlAimed at improving the efficiency of the economy and increasing its international competitiveness by removing rigidities
Maintaining sufficient foreign exchange reserves and keeping prices in checkReforms in industry, finance, taxation, trade and the public sector

The structural reforms are grouped under three heads: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

notes.heading: Liberalisation: industrial and financial sector reforms
notes.html:
Liberalisation means removing unnecessary government controls and restrictions so that the economy can function more freely.

Industrial sector

  • Abolition of industrial licensing for almost all products except a few such as alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, and drugs and pharmaceuticals (the list has been shortened further since).
  • Reduced reservation for the public sector: industries reserved for the public sector were cut down to a few, such as defence equipment, atomic energy generation and railway transport (the list has been narrowed further over time).
  • Many goods de-reserved from the small-scale sector.
  • Market forces were allowed to determine prices in many industries.

Financial sector

  • The role of the RBI was changed from a regulator to a facilitator of the financial sector, allowing it to take many decisions on its own without consulting the RBI.
  • Private sector banks, both Indian and foreign, were allowed to enter, and the foreign investment limit in banks was raised.
  • Banks were given freedom to open new branches (subject to conditions) and to rationalise existing ones.
  • Foreign institutional investors such as merchant bankers, mutual funds and pension funds were allowed to invest in Indian financial markets.

notes.heading: Liberalisation: tax, foreign exchange and trade reforms
notes.html:
Tax reforms (fiscal policy)

  • Rates of personal income tax and corporation tax were reduced and the tax structure simplified, on the belief that moderate rates encourage savings and voluntary disclosure of income.
  • Indirect taxes were reformed to create a common national market; the Goods and Services Tax (GST), launched in July 2017, replaced many central and state indirect taxes with a single tax ('one nation, one tax').

Foreign exchange reforms

  • In 1991 the rupee was devalued against foreign currencies as an immediate measure to resolve the BoP crisis; this raised the inflow of foreign exchange.
  • The exchange rate was gradually freed to be determined by the market, with RBI intervention to curb volatility (managed floating).

Trade and investment policy reforms

  • Dismantling of quantitative restrictions on imports and exports; these were fully removed from April 2001.
  • Reduction of tariff rates.
  • Removal of import licensing except for hazardous and environmentally sensitive industries.
  • Export duties removed to make Indian goods competitive.
  • Ceilings on foreign investment were raised in many sectors.

notes.heading: Privatisation and disinvestment
notes.html:
Privatisation means shedding the ownership or management of a government-owned enterprise. It occurs by (a) withdrawal of the government from ownership and management, or (b) outright sale of public sector companies. Sale of a part of the government's equity in PSUs to the public is called disinvestment.

  • Purpose: improve financial discipline and efficiency of PSUs, bring in private capital and managerial skill, and raise resources for the government. It was also expected to encourage FDI.
  • Ratna status: to make efficient and profitable PSUs more competitive, the government granted them greater managerial and operational autonomy under the status of Maharatna, Navratna (introduced 1997) and Miniratna. Examples of Maharatnas include ONGC, NTPC, Indian Oil Corporation and SAIL. With autonomy these companies expanded and improved their performance.

Criticism: assets of PSUs were often undervalued and sold cheaply; proceeds were frequently used to meet revenue shortfalls rather than to develop PSUs or build social infrastructure.

notes.heading: Globalisation, outsourcing and the WTO
notes.html:
Globalisation means integrating the economy of a country with the world economy, through free flow of goods, services, capital, technology and to some extent people, so that the world becomes more interdependent ('a borderless world').

Outsourcing

A company hires regular services from external sources, mostly from other countries, which it earlier provided internally. Examples: legal advice, computer services, advertising, call centres (voice-based BPO), record keeping, accountancy, banking services, music recording, film editing, teaching and medical transcription. India is a favoured destination because of its large pool of skilled, English-speaking workers available at low wages and because of the IT revolution that allows data to be sent cheaply and instantly.

World Trade Organisation (WTO)

  • Founded in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT, 1948). India is a founding member.
  • Aim: establish a rule-based trading regime, reduce tariff and non-tariff barriers, provide greater market access to all members, and enlarge production and trade in goods and services while making optimum use of world resources and protecting the environment.
  • Agreements cover trade in goods and services as well as intellectual property rights (TRIPS) and trade-related investment measures.
  • Criticism: developed countries continue to protect their agriculture with subsidies, while developing countries are pressured to open their markets.

notes.heading: Appraisal: achievements of the reforms
notes.html:
• Growth: GDP growth rose compared with the pre-reform period, driven mainly by the services sector.
  • Foreign investment: FDI and foreign portfolio investment increased many times.
  • Foreign exchange reserves: rose sharply from the crisis level; India now holds one of the largest foreign exchange reserves in the world.
  • Exports: India emerged as an exporter of auto parts, engineering goods, IT services, textiles and pharmaceuticals.
  • Prices: inflation was generally kept under better control than in the crisis years.
  • Competition and choice: consumers gained from better quality goods and wider choice; telecom and civil aviation expanded rapidly.

notes.heading: Appraisal: shortcomings and criticisms
notes.html:
• Neglect of agriculture: public investment in agriculture, especially in irrigation, power, roads, market linkages and research, declined. Removal of fertiliser subsidy (in part) raised input costs; reduced import duties exposed farmers to international competition; export orientation shifted land from food crops to cash crops, putting pressure on food grain prices.
  • Industrial slowdown: cheap imports reduced demand for domestic industrial goods; infrastructure such as power supply remained inadequate; developed countries kept non-tariff barriers against Indian goods.
  • Disinvestment concerns: undervaluation of PSU assets and use of the money to plug deficits.
  • Fiscal policies: tax cuts aimed at higher compliance did not always raise revenue; competition to attract foreign investment led to tax incentives that reduced revenue.
  • Jobless growth: growth in output did not generate a corresponding growth in employment, especially of good quality jobs.
  • Uneven benefits: gains went mainly to high-income groups and urban areas, widening inequality.

Later developments: other reforms include demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes in November 2016 (aimed at curbing black money and counterfeit currency and promoting digital transactions) and the introduction of GST in 2017.

keyTerms.definition: The set of economic reforms based on liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation announced by the Government of India in July 1991.
Removal of unnecessary government controls and restrictions on economic activity.
Transfer of ownership or management of a government enterprise to the private sector.
Sale of a part of the government's equity in public sector enterprises to the public or private investors.
Integration of a country's economy with the world economy through free flow of goods, services, capital and technology.
Short-term measures to correct the balance of payments and control inflation.
Long-term measures to improve efficiency and international competitiveness by removing rigidities in the economy.
Hiring of regular services from external sources, often from other countries, that a company earlier produced internally.
World Trade Organisation, founded in 1995 as successor to GATT, to set rules for international trade and reduce trade barriers.
Limits on the quantity of goods that can be imported or exported, such as quotas.
Deliberate reduction in the external value of a currency by the government, as done with the rupee in 1991.
A status given since 1997 to selected profitable public sector enterprises, granting them greater financial and managerial autonomy.

mcqs.q: In 1991, India's foreign exchange reserves were sufficient to pay for imports of only about:
mcqs.explanation: Reserves fell so low in 1991 that they could cover only about two weeks of imports, which triggered the crisis.

mcqs.q: The WTO was founded in 1995 as the successor to:
mcqs.explanation: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (1948) was replaced by the WTO in 1995.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a stabilisation measure?
options: Opening the banking sector to private banks
Measures to control inflation and correct the balance of payments
mcqs.explanation: Stabilisation measures are short-term steps to correct the BoP and curb inflation; the rest are long-term structural reforms.

mcqs.q: After 1991 the role of the RBI changed from:
options: Lender of last resort to currency authority
mcqs.explanation: Financial sector reforms aimed to let banks and institutions take more decisions themselves, with the RBI acting as a facilitator.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): India became a favourite destination for outsourcing after the reforms.
Reason (R): India has a large pool of skilled, English-speaking workers available at relatively low wages.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Low-cost skilled manpower, together with the IT revolution, made India attractive for outsourcing. R explains A.

mcqs.q: Which of the following industries remained reserved for the public sector after 1991?
mcqs.explanation: Only a few sectors such as defence equipment, atomic energy generation and railway transport remained reserved; steel, telecom and aviation were opened to private firms.

mcqs.q:
Read the statements:
Statement 1: Disinvestment means the sale of a part of the government's equity in PSUs.
Statement 2: The proceeds of disinvestment have always been used only for developing PSUs.
options: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true
mcqs.explanation: Statement 1 is the definition of disinvestment. Critics point out that the proceeds were often used to meet revenue shortfalls, so Statement 2 is false.

mcqs.q: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced in India in:
mcqs.explanation: GST came into force on 1 July 2017. November 2016 was demonetisation, and April 2001 was the removal of quantitative restrictions.

mcqs.q: Which sector contributed most to the higher growth after the reforms?
mcqs.explanation: Post-reform growth was largely services-led (IT, finance, telecom, trade), while agriculture's growth slowed.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a criticism of the reforms with respect to agriculture?
options: Agriculture received a sharp rise in public investment
Food grain production was given priority over cash crops
Public investment in agricultural infrastructure declined
mcqs.explanation: Critics note that public investment in irrigation, power, roads and research fell, which hurt agricultural growth.

mcqs.q: Quantitative restrictions on imports in India were fully removed from:
mcqs.explanation: QRs on imports of manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products were fully removed from April 2001.

mcqs.q: The 1991 loan to India came mainly from:
options: The Asian Development Bank and WTO
The IBRD (World Bank) and the IMF
mcqs.explanation: India approached the World Bank and the IMF and received about US$7 billion, with conditions to liberalise the economy.

questions.answerHtml: Outsourcing is the practice of a company hiring regular services, such as call centres, accounting or software support, from external sources, mostly from other countries, instead of providing them internally.

questions.q: Name the two international agencies from which India borrowed during the 1991 crisis.
questions.answerHtml: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank) and the International Monetary Fund.

questions.q: Distinguish between stabilisation and structural reform measures.
questions.answerHtml:
Stabilisation measuresStructural reform measures
Short-term measuresLong-term measures
Aim to correct the balance of payments and control inflationAim to improve efficiency and international competitiveness
Example: keeping sufficient forex reserves, controlling rising pricesExample: delicensing, financial sector reform, trade liberalisation, privatisation

questions.q: Why did India need economic reforms in 1991? Give any three reasons.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Fiscal deficit: persistent excess of government spending over revenue led to heavy borrowing and rising interest payments.
  2. Balance of payments crisis: imports far exceeded exports; foreign exchange reserves fell so low that they could pay for only about two weeks of imports, and India found it hard to repay its foreign debt.
  3. High inflation and inefficient public sector: prices rose sharply and many public enterprises made losses, while the licence-permit system stifled efficiency. External shocks such as the Gulf War worsened the situation.

questions.q: 'Indian agriculture has been adversely affected by the reform process.' Defend or refute.
questions.answerHtml:
The statement is defended.

  1. Fall in public investment: public spending on agricultural infrastructure such as irrigation, power, roads, market linkages and research declined.
  2. Rising input costs: partial removal of fertiliser subsidies raised the cost of production, hurting small and marginal farmers.
  3. Global competition: reduction in import duties on agricultural products exposed Indian farmers to competition from heavily subsidised producers in developed countries.
  4. Shift to cash crops: export-oriented policy shifted land from food crops to cash crops, raising food grain prices.

As a result agricultural growth slowed in the post-reform period compared with industry and services.

questions.q: Explain the role of the WTO. Why has India been a member despite criticisms?
questions.answerHtml:
Role of the WTO:

  • Establishes a rule-based trading system in which nations cannot place arbitrary restrictions on trade.
  • Reduces tariff and non-tariff barriers and provides greater market access to all members.
  • Covers trade in goods and services and intellectual property rights.
  • Settles trade disputes among members.

Why India remains a member: India is a founding member and participates to secure fair rules for developing countries. Membership gives it access to world markets for its exports, a forum to raise the issue of farm subsidies in developed countries, and a dispute settlement mechanism. Staying outside would isolate India from the global trading system.

questions.q: Discuss the main reforms introduced in the industrial and trade sectors under the New Economic Policy 1991.
questions.answerHtml:
Industrial sector reforms

  • Delicensing: industrial licensing was abolished for almost all products except a short list such as alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace and drugs and pharmaceuticals.
  • Public sector reservation reduced: only a few industries, such as defence equipment, atomic energy generation and railway transport, remained reserved for the public sector.
  • De-reservation: many goods earlier reserved for small-scale industries were opened to all.
  • Price freedom: market forces were allowed to determine prices in many industries.

Trade and investment reforms

  • Removal of quantitative restrictions: quotas on imports and exports were dismantled; they were fully removed from April 2001.
  • Tariff reduction: import duties were lowered to make Indian industry more competitive.
  • Import licensing abolished except for hazardous and environmentally sensitive industries.
  • Export promotion: export duties were removed.
  • Foreign investment: limits on foreign equity were raised and the process of approval simplified.
  • Exchange rate: the rupee was devalued in 1991 and later moved to a market-determined rate.

These reforms aimed to make Indian industry more efficient and integrate it with world markets.

questions.q: Critically appraise the economic reforms introduced in India since 1991.
questions.answerHtml:
Achievements

  • Higher growth: GDP growth rose above pre-reform rates, led by the services sector.
  • Foreign investment and reserves: FDI and portfolio inflows increased many times; foreign exchange reserves rose from the crisis level to among the largest in the world.
  • Exports: India became a major exporter of IT services, auto parts, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals and textiles.
  • Competition and consumer choice improved; inflation was generally kept under better control than in the crisis years.

Failures and criticisms

  • Neglect of agriculture: reduced public investment, higher input costs and global competition slowed farm growth.
  • Industrial slowdown: cheap imports and inadequate infrastructure hurt domestic industry; non-tariff barriers abroad limited exports.
  • Disinvestment: PSU assets were sometimes undervalued and proceeds used to bridge deficits.
  • Jobless growth: employment, especially in the formal sector, did not grow in proportion to output.
  • Inequality: benefits went mainly to urban and high-income groups.

Conclusion: the reforms rescued India from the 1991 crisis and raised growth, but their benefits have been uneven; agriculture, employment and equity require greater attention.
